doctrine: POSITIONING = deliberate context-setting. Not messaging. Not tagline. Context that lets customers instantly categorize your offer and understand its value. Six components must be resolved in this order: (1) Competitive alternatives: what the best-fit customer would use if you did not exist, NOT who you fear as a startup competitor. Most common real alternative is spreadsheets/manual process. (2) Unique attributes: features/capabilities you have that the alternatives do not. Must be provable, not aspirational. Qualitative claims ('great service') are worthless without third-party proof. (3) Value: what those attributes enable for customers in their goals, not just what the feature does. Feature > Benefit > Value chain. Reduce to 1-4 value clusters. (4) Best-fit target: the customers who buy fast, never ask for discounts, refer others, and fight you if you try to take the product away. Start narrow, broaden only when you have evidence. (5) Market category: the frame of reference you declare. This triggers assumptions about competitors, features, and pricing. Choosing wrong is catastrophic. Three positioning styles: (a) Head to Head: enter existing well-defined market, claim to be best for all buyers. Only viable if you are current leader or there is no clear leader yet. (b) Big Fish, Small Pond: enter existing category but dominate a subsegment with distinct unmet needs. Best path for most small players. Sub-segment must be identifiable, big enough to hit revenue goals, and have a need the category leader structurally cannot serve well. (c) Create a New Game: define an entirely new market category. Requires: massive market shift (tech/regulatory/behavioral), ability to educate market on the problem before selling the solution, long-term commitment and capital, clear 'why now' answer. Most difficult; best rewards if executed. Bonus component: Relevant trend. Optional but powerful. Trend must link directly to your market category and product value -- never lead with trend as a substitute for category. Market category = what you are; trend = why this matters right now. Execution after positioning: (1) Capture positioning in a full-detail document AND a one-page canvas. Never just a statement. (2) Build a sales story arc: problem definition > current-solution gaps > 'perfect world' > product intro with market category > value themes > call to action. (3) Write a master messaging document as baseline so downstream copy does not drift. (4) Let pricing reinforce positioning (niche/premium pricing expected in specialized categories). (5) Review positioning every 6 months or after any major competitive/regulatory/technology event. Positioning Baggage Rule: founders are trapped in the product they set out to build. Explicitly name and surface current positioning assumptions before the exercise. Kill the default. Positioning Statement is explicitly condemned: assumes answers, reinforces status quo, produces unusable output, is never operationalized.
contradictions: OS language sometimes conflates 'positioning' with 'messaging' or 'voice.' Dunford is explicit: positioning is upstream of messaging. Messaging is the output, not positioning itself. If OS uses these interchangeably, it corrupts the process.

OS may assume broad audience targeting improves reach. Dunford is explicit: broader positioning reduces close rates, increases churn, and attracts poor-fit buyers. Narrowing to best-fit customers is the more efficient path to revenue.

Trend-first framing ('AI-empowered X', 'sharing economy for Y') is common in OS copy guidance. Dunford explicitly warns this creates confused customers. Market category must be established first; trend layered second.

Positioning Statement exercises -- if any OS templates reference this format (FOR [target] YOUR [product] IS A [category] WHICH [benefit] UNLIKE [competitor]...) -- are explicitly called out as useless and potentially harmful. Dunford advocates replacing with the 10-step process and a positioning canvas.
chunk_accuracy_note: The four prior chunks accurately capture the philosophical core (context-setting, five components, category choice, strengths-first) but miss the entire operational half of the book: the 10-step sequenced process, the three positioning styles (Head to Head / Big Fish Small Pond / Create a New Game) with their specific use conditions, the Sales Story arc, the Positioning Canvas format, the messaging document discipline, the 6-month review cadence, the explicit condemnation of the Positioning Statement, and the Positioning Baggage concept. The chunks deliver correct principles but zero executable procedure -- which is the book's actual competitive advantage over every other positioning text.
gate_candidates: Before finalizing any SNIPED offer description or service page: run the 5-component positioning check (alternatives, attributes, value, best-fit, market category) in order. Gate passes only when all five are explicitly defined.

Before claiming a trend in any SNIPED copy (e.g., 'AI-powered,' 'editorial,' 'new luxury'): verify the market category is stated first and the trend has a direct, demonstrable link to the product's value. Trend-only framing fails the gate.
workflow_candidates: 10-Step Positioning Workshop: (1) List best-fit customers. (2) Form cross-functional team. (3) Surface and name current positioning baggage. (4) List true competitive alternatives from customer POV. (5) List unique attributes vs. those alternatives. (6) Map attributes to value themes (1-4 clusters). (7) Identify who cares most about that value. (8) Choose market frame of reference (Head to Head / Big Fish Small Pond / Create a New Game). (9) Optionally layer a relevant trend. (10) Capture in positioning canvas + detailed document. Then: build sales story arc, write master messaging doc.

Positioning Review Trigger: every 6 months OR when a major competitor enters, a regulation changes, or a new technology shifts buyer assumptions -- restart at Step 4 (competitive alternatives) and re-run the downstream chain.
notes: Book is B2B/tech-dominant in its case studies (database, CRM, SaaS), but the positioning logic is category-agnostic and maps cleanly to SNIPED's service positioning challenge. The 'Big Fish, Small Pond' style directly mirrors the SNIPED strategic move: don't compete against all photographers, dominate the 'editorial brand photography for LA founders' subsegment where SNIPED's specific combination of aesthetic lineage, compositing capability, and cultural fluency creates unbeatable differentiation. The Joshua Bell subway experiment is the single most useful teaching story in the book for SNIPED context: world-class product, wrong context, $32 in 45 minutes.
